title: Becoming a Whisky Educator | Craft Beer School
desc: How to become a whisky educator in India: the knowledge, the qualifications, running responsible tastings and finding your audience.
teaser: Teaching whisky is half knowledge and half running a room. Both can be learned.
standfirst: Whisky educators run tastings, train bar and sales teams and teach courses. The job rewards deep knowledge, but it rewards clear teaching more. Here is what the work involves and how people build a career in it.
sections:
The title covers several jobs. Some educators work for a drinks company, training sales teams, bartenders and retail staff on the portfolio. Some work independently, running consumer tastings and corporate sessions. Some teach formal courses toward qualifications. Many do a mix of all three.

What links them is the job of turning a complicated subject into something a room can understand in an hour or two. That means knowing the subject well enough to simplify it without making it wrong.

Accuracy is the foundation. An educator who gets the basics wrong in front of an audience loses it quickly, especially if one person in the room knows more than they let on.

  • Production. Malting, mashing, fermentation to a wash of around 8% ABV, pot and column distillation, cuts and maturation.
  • Definitions. Scotch matures at least three years in oak in Scotland and is bottled at no less than 40% ABV. Bourbon uses at least 51% corn and new charred oak containers. Irish whiskey matures at least three years on the island of Ireland.
  • Regions and styles. What distinguishes Islay from Speyside, Japanese from Scotch, Indian single malt from molasses based spirit.
  • Sensory. How to nose and taste and how to help others put words to what they find.

Our guide to whisky label terms is a good test: if you can explain every term on it from memory, you have the base.

No licence is needed to teach whisky, but credentials help you get hired and trusted. The Wine and Spirit Education Trust (WSET) offers spirits qualifications at several levels, taught through approved providers. The Institute of Brewing and Distilling (IBD) offers production focused qualifications, starting with the General Certificate in Distilling. Each suits a different kind of educator: WSET leans toward product and tasting, the IBD toward how spirit is made.

A short practical distilling course fills the gap many tasting focused educators have. Being able to describe a spirit still from having seen one run changes how you teach cuts and new make.

Responsible practice is part of the craft, not an afterthought. A good tasting:

  • Pours small measures, typically 15 to 20 ml per whisky across a flight of five or six samples.
  • Puts water and spittoons on every table, with food available.
  • Paces the session so nobody feels rushed to finish a glass.
  • Welcomes people who only want to nose. Never pressures anyone to drink.
  • Reminds guests not to drive afterwards and helps arrange transport where needed.

In India, check the local rules before running a paid tasting. Venue licences and the rules on serving alcohol at events vary by state. Corporate sessions should sit within the client's own alcohol policy.

Knowing whisky and teaching it are different things. Good educators plan each session around three or four ideas, not thirty facts. They use the glass in front of people as the lesson: nose the ex-bourbon cask whisky, then the sherry cask one. The difference teaches cask influence better than any slide.

They also read the room. A group of new sales hires needs vocabulary and confidence. A whisky club wants depth and debate. The same flight can serve both if the framing changes. Our guide to hosting a whisky tasting covers the practical setup.

Whisky rules and the market change. Categories get new definitions, regions gain new distilleries and labelling rules are revised. An educator who taught the same slides for ten years will eventually teach something out of date.

Build a habit of checking. Read the current rules for the categories you teach, from Scotch and Irish whiskey to bourbon. Visit distilleries when you can. Ask production staff what has changed in their process. Keep a source list for every number you use in a session, so if someone challenges a figure you can show where it came from.

Be honest about what you do not know. Saying you will check and come back is far better than inventing an answer in front of a room. Audiences forgive gaps. They do not forgive being misled.

Most educators start with a related job: bartending, brand ambassador work, retail or sales at a drinks company. They build up teaching hours with small groups, gather feedback and slowly earn a reputation. Writing helps too. A clear blog or tasting notes that show you can explain things well open doors.

Start small this month. Plan a 45 minute session on one idea, such as how the cask changes whisky, using three samples. Write down exactly what you want people to understand at the end. If you find gaps in how you would explain the production side, fill those before you stand in front of a room.
faqs: Do I need a qualification to teach whisky?
No licence is required, but recognised qualifications such as WSET spirits awards or IBD distilling certificates help you get hired and trusted.
How much whisky should each guest get at a tasting?
Small measures of around 15 to 20 ml per whisky across five or six samples are typical, with water and spittoons on every table.
Can I run paid whisky tastings in India?
Rules on serving alcohol at events vary by state and venue licence. Check the current local rules before charging for a tasting.
